module: Pancreatitis, Cystic Fibrosis and Biliary Atresia

steps.say: Pancreatitis in children hides behind vague tummy ache and vomiting, so apply the rule of two out of three. Typical epigastric pain, enzymes three times normal, and matching scans: any two seal the diagnosis. No single feature suffices alone. The necrosis and walled collection drawing here shows exactly the imaging end of that triad, the structural damage the third criterion describes.
steps.tx: Apply the **NASPGHAN diagnostic triad** strictly (the North American paediatric pancreas definition). Pediatric acute pancreatitis requires at least 2 of 3 criteria: abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin, serum lipase or amylase at least 3 times upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging findings. Meeting only one criterion means watching and retesting, not labelling. Document which two criteria are met, because the pair chosen steers whether enzymes or scans lead follow up.

vis.alt: Necrotic pancreas, fat saponification, and a fibrous capsule around a collection.
vis.caption: Necrosis and a walled collection in acute pancreatitis. StewardMD original.

steps.say: When both enzymes are up, believe the lipase. It climbs higher, stays high for eight to fourteen days against three to five for amylase, and tops ninety percent sensitivity in children. Amylase fades early and rises in non pancreatic conditions like parotitis too. So a late presenter with normal amylase but high lipase still has pancreatitis until proven otherwise.
steps.tx: Prefer **lipase diagnostic superiority** in testing strategy. Serum lipase remains elevated longer (8-14 days versus 3-5 days for amylase) and provides significantly higher sensitivity (over 90%) and specificity in children. Order lipase first in every suspected case, repeat it rather than amylase for trending, and interpret isolated amylase rises cautiously since salivary and tubal sources confound it. Normal lipase after two weeks does not exclude resolving disease already diagnosed on criteria.

steps.say: Children do not follow the adult alcohol and gallstone script, so run through the paediatric culprit list. Biliary sludge and stones cause a fifth to a third, medicines like valproate and asparaginase up to a quarter, and handlebar blows to the belly about one in seven. Infections and structural anomalies fill the remainder. Finding the trigger prevents the next attack far better than any drug.
steps.tx: Work through the **etiology spectrum in children** systematically. Biliary disease (20-30%, sludge and stones), medications (valproate, asparaginase, 6-mercaptopurine and steroids causing 15-25%), blunt abdominal trauma (handlebar injury compressing the gland, 10-15%), and systemic infection are primary triggers. Image the biliary tree in every first attack, review the drug chart ruthlessly, and ask about bicycle handlebar impact specifically, since children forget the blow that injured the gland.

steps.say: Starving the inflamed gland is outdated and harmful, so feed early. A low fat meal or a nasojejunal drip within twenty four to forty eight hours calms the inflammatory storm and shortens the stay. The gut barrier stays alive on food, keeping bacteria out of the necrotic pancreas. Only ileus, blockage or fistula justify keeping the child nil by mouth.
steps.tx: Start **early enteral nutrition** within 24-48 hours (oral low-fat feeds or nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes). Early enteral feeding is superior to bowel rest, reducing length of stay and systemic inflammatory response by preserving gut barrier function (the intestinal seal against bacterial translocation). Advance from low-fat solids as pain settles, reserving parenteral nutrition (vein feeding) for true intolerance. Document intake daily, because underfed pancreatitis recovers slowest.

steps.say: An inflamed pancreas leaks fluid into the tissues, so resuscitate with purpose, not drips and hopes. Lactated Ringer's at one and a half to two times maintenance through the first day keeps the gland perfused and necrosis at bay. Watch urine output, heart rate and belly girth hourly, easing back once targets hold. Overfilling a child is as dangerous as underfilling, so titrate constantly.
steps.tx: Give the **fluid resuscitation target** as targeted crystalloid with lactated Ringer solution (the balanced salt fluid) at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance volume during the initial 24 hours. This prevents hypoperfusion and pancreatic necrosis (gland death from blood loss) without drowning the lungs. Reassess with blood urea, hematocrit and urine output, slowing when targets are met and switching early to enteral intake. Avoid routine normal saline excess, which worsens acidosis in inflamed children.

steps.say: One attack in a child deserves a genetic thought, and repeated attacks demand it. Dominant trypsinogen mutations drive the trypsin that digests the gland itself, while SPINK1, CFTR and CTRC variants remove the brakes. A strong family history, early onset or progression to chronicity should trigger testing and counselling. Naming the gene changes screening for siblings and expectations for the years ahead.
steps.tx: Test **genetic mutations in chronic pancreatitis** when attacks recur. Recurrent and chronic pancreatitis in children is driven by mutations in PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen, autosomal dominant), SPINK1 (trypsin inhibitor), CFTR (chloride channel shared with cystic fibrosis), and CTRC (chymotrypsin regulator). Refer early-onset, familial or rapidly chronic cases for genetics and counselling, and screen siblings of PRSS1 carriers. Gene positive children need lifelong surveillance, because chronic calcific disease and diabetes follow many of them.

steps.say: Not every fluid collection needs a drain; the calendar matters enormously. A true pseudocyst wears a fibrous but non epithelial wall that only matures around four weeks after necrotising injury. Early walled collections are not ready for drainage and often resolve alone. The transgastric stent drawing shows the mature solution: a window through the stomach into a ripe collection. Drain the infected or compressing cyst, and watch the quiet one.
steps.tx: Time the **pancreatic pseudocyst timing** rule correctly. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a fibrous non-epithelialised fluid collection (a fluid sac without a true lining) developing at least 4 weeks following acute necrotizing pancreatitis. Collections before this lack a drainable wall and usually regress with supportive care alone. Image at four weeks to confirm maturation, drain infected, enlarging or obstructing pseudocysts endoscopically as drawn here, and follow small silent ones to resolution.

vis.alt: Transgastric stent draining walled-off pancreatic necrosis into the stomach.
vis.caption: A transgastric stent into a walled-off collection. The capsule is why the delay is about 4 weeks when the patient can wait. The drawing does not show a patient who is deteriorating, and that patient is not held to the calendar. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: When pain owns the child's life despite medicines, scopes and enzymes, removing the battlefield becomes kindness. Total pancreatectomy with the islets salvaged and reinfused into the liver trades chronic agony for manageable diabetes. Reserve it for truly intractable chronic pancreatitis after every lesser therapy has failed. The decision belongs in a specialist centre with pain, endocrine and surgical teams around one table.
steps.tx: Reserve the **TPIAT indication** for end-stage pain. Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TPIAT, removing the whole gland while reinfusing the insulin making islets into the liver) is indicated for intractable pain in chronic pancreatitis refractory to medical and endoscopic therapy. Candidates have exhausted analgesia, enzyme replacement, duct drainage and celiac blocks without relief, and accept post-surgical diabetes as the price of freedom from pain. Refer before narcotic dependence cements itself, since earlier operation preserves more islet function.
